Mitigating Collaborative Semantic ID Staleness in Generative Retrieval

Conference: Proceedings of the 49th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval; July 20–24, 2026; Melbourne, VIC, Australia.Proceedings of the 49th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR ’26), July 20–24, 2026, Melbourne, VIC, AustraliaISBN: 979-8-4007-2599-9/2026/07DOI: 10.1145/3805712.3809877CCS: Information systems Recommender systemsCCS: Information systems Retrieval models and ranking
Vladimir Baikalov email: deadinside@itmo.ru Affiliation: AI VK, Moscow, Russia Affiliation: ITMO University, St. Petersburg, Russia , Iskander Bagautdinov email: iskbaga@itmo.ru Affiliation: ITMO University, St. Petersburg, Russia and Sergey Muravyov email: smuravyov@itmo.ru Affiliation: ITMO University, St. Petersburg, Russia
2026
Abstract.

Generative retrieval with Semantic IDs (SIDs) assigns each item a discrete identifier and treats retrieval as a sequence generation problem rather than a nearest-neighbor search. While content-only SIDs are stable, they do not take into account user-item interaction patterns, so recent systems construct interaction-informed SIDs. However, as interaction patterns drift over time, these identifiers become stale, i.e., their collaborative semantics no longer match recent logs.

Prior work typically assumes a fixed SID vocabulary during fine-tuning, or treats SID refresh as a full rebuild that requires retraining. However, SID staleness under temporal drift is rarely analyzed explicitly. To bridge this gap, we study SID staleness under strict chronological evaluation and propose a lightweight, model-agnostic SID alignment update.

Given refreshed SIDs derived from recent logs, we align them to the existing SID vocabulary so the retriever checkpoint remains compatible, enabling standard warm-start fine-tuning without a full rebuild-and-retrain pipeline. Across three public benchmarks, our update consistently improves Recall@K and nDCG@K at high cutoffs over naive fine-tuning with stale SIDs and reduces retriever-training compute by approximately 8–9 times compared to full retraining.

Keywords: 
Recommender Systems, Sequential Recommendation, Generative Retrieval, Semantic IDs, Distribution Drift

1. Introduction

Large-scale recommender and search systems rely on retrieval to select a small candidate set from massive catalogs (Covington et al., 2016; Borisyuk et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2025). Generative retrieval with Semantic IDs (SIDs) offers an alternative to embedding-based retrieval. Instead of retrieving items via vector similarity, each item is assigned a short token sequence, which the model generates from the user context (Rajput et al., 2023).

A key design choice is how to construct SIDs. Content-only SIDs (derived from metadata or multimodal features) are stable and effective in cold-start scenarios (Singh et al., 2024), but can miss behavioral structure captured in interaction logs (Wang et al., 2024a). Recent systems therefore build interaction-informed SIDs, often improving retrieval quality (He et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2025).

In practical settings, collaborative patterns are non-stationary: user interests, item popularity, and logging policies evolve over time, motivating periodic SID refreshes to capture the latest collaborative structure. Yet refreshing SIDs introduces a challenge: new token assignments may become incompatible with the retriever’s previously learned output space. Despite its practical relevance, this issue has received limited attention in prior works. As a result, practitioners typically face a trade-off: (i) keep SIDs fixed and finetune on new logs, accumulating SID–behavior mismatch, or (ii) refresh SIDs and retrain from scratch at high compute cost (He et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2025).

However, SID staleness under temporal drift has not been systematically quantified. To bridge this gap, we quantify interaction-informed SID staleness under strict chronological evaluation and propose a lightweight, model-agnostic alignment update that keeps refreshed identifiers checkpoint-compatible. Our contributions are:

  • •

    We quantify the degradation caused by stale interaction-informed SIDs under temporal drift.

  • •

    We propose a lightweight, model-agnostic SID alignment update that enables warm-start finetuning with refreshed identifiers.

  • •

    On three public temporal benchmarks, we show that alignment improves over stale-SID finetuning and is competitive with full retraining while reducing retriever training compute by up to 8–9 times.

2. Related Work

Generative Retrieval. Generative retrieval frames candidate generation as sequence modeling, where a model directly decodes item identifiers (De Cao et al., 2021; Tay et al., 2022; Mehta et al., 2023). A prominent line of work trains generative retrievers to autoregressively generate item IDs from user context (Tang et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024a; Sun et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022), while subsequent work focuses on scaling and production-oriented training and inference recipes (Pradeep et al., 2023).

Semantic IDs and item tokenization. A central component of generative retrieval is item tokenization, which maps each item to a short sequence of discrete tokens (Semantic ID) for generation. TIGER (Rajput et al., 2023) popularized learned Semantic IDs via residual quantization (e.g., RQ-VAE (Lee et al., 2022)) over item content embeddings. Subsequent works focus on improving SID quality (Wang et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2024b; Tang et al., 2024; Vandenhirtz et al., 2026; Si et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024b) and show that SID construction is often decisive for downstream retrieval performance. In particular, LETTER (Wang et al., 2024a) introduces interaction-informed tokenization by adding collaborative regularization to the quantizer training objective. However, existing tokenization methods typically assume a static SID vocabulary and do not explicitly address how to preserve compatibility when SIDs are refreshed over time. In contrast, we focus on the SID update step under temporal drift: refreshing interaction-informed SIDs while reusing an existing retriever checkpoint.

Industry applications of Semantic IDs. Several industrial systems report applying Semantic IDs at scale (Yang et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025), combining SID tokenization with large generative backbones and production constraints (e.g., constrained decoding and efficient serving). Representative examples include PLUM (He et al., 2026) and OneRec (Deng et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025a; Zhou et al., 2025b), and Spotify’s work on unified generative search and recommendation (Penha et al., 2024). While these works demonstrate practical value at scale, they largely focus on SID construction and training/serving recipes, leaving checkpoint-compatible SID refresh and continual adaptation under temporal drift underexplored.

3. Proposed Approach

We study how to refresh Semantic IDs (SIDs) in generative retrieval for sequential recommendation while preserving compatibility with an existing checkpoint. In real-world deployment scenarios, SID-based retrievers are often finetuned on fresh logs while keeping SIDs fixed, which can make interaction-informed identifiers stale as collaborative patterns drift over time (He et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2025). Our goal is to incorporate fresh interaction signals into SIDs while keeping the deployed retriever warm-startable, avoiding a full rebuild-and-retrain pipeline.

3.1. Problem Setup

We consider the retrieval (candidate generation) stage in sequential recommendation. Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} and ℐ\mathcal{I} denote the sets of users and items. Each user u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U} is represented by a time-ordered interaction sequence Su=(iu,1,…,iu,|Su|)S_{u}=(i_{u,1},\dots,i_{u,|S_{u}|}). Given SuS_{u}, retrieval returns a candidate set of items (typically hundreds to thousands), deferring fine-grained ordering to a downstream ranker.

We focus on a SID-based generative retriever, where each item i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I} is assigned a SID represented as a token sequence of length L,

(1) 𝐳i=(zi,1,…,zi,L),zi,ℓ∈𝒱ℓ,\mathbf{z}_{i}=(z_{i,1},\dots,z_{i,L}),\quad z_{i,\ell}\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell},

where 𝒱ℓ\mathcal{V}_{\ell} is the vocabulary of the ℓ\ell-th codebook. Conditioned on user context, the retriever generates SID tokens and retrieves candidate items via a SID-to-item mapping.

Crucially, the retriever is tied to the SID space via token embeddings and distributions over {𝒱ℓ}ℓ=1L\{\mathcal{V}_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}. Thus, rebuilding SIDs reassigns tokens and makes checkpoint reuse non-trivial. Without special handling, warm-start finetuning can be unstable and is often avoided in favor of retraining from scratch. Conversely, keeping SIDs fixed while finetuning on fresh interactions can lead to stale identifiers that no longer reflect the latest collaborative structure. Accordingly, we focus on SID update procedures that inject fresh signals from new logs while preserving the original token space, so the retriever can be warm-started rather than fully retrained.

3.2. Semantic-ID Alignment Update

We assume two SID assignments over a largely shared item space: (i) an old SID token assignment produced previously, and (ii) a new SID token assignment rebuilt from fresher logs. For each item ii,

(2) 𝐳iold=(zi,1old,…,zi,Lold),𝐳inew=(zi,1new,…,zi,Lnew).\mathbf{z}^{\text{old}}_{i}=(z^{\text{old}}_{i,1},\dots,z^{\text{old}}_{i,L}),\qquad\mathbf{z}^{\text{new}}_{i}=(z^{\text{new}}_{i,1},\dots,z^{\text{new}}_{i,L}).

Our goal is to construct a bijective function ϕ\phi that aligns the new SIDs into the old token space, producing updated identifiers

(3) 𝐳~i=(z~i,1,…,z~i,L),z~i,ℓ=ϕℓ​(zi,ℓnew),\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}=(\tilde{z}_{i,1},\dots,\tilde{z}_{i,L}),\qquad\tilde{z}_{i,\ell}=\phi_{\ell}\!\left(z^{\text{new}}_{i,\ell}\right),

where each ϕℓ\phi_{\ell} is a one-to-one mapping of tokens within the same codebook position (codebook-consistent alignment). Intuitively, 𝐳~i\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i} preserves the token space expected by the existing model, while reflecting updated collaborative structure captured by 𝐳inew\mathbf{z}^{\text{new}}_{i}.

To construct ϕ\phi, we use items that appear in both the old and new tokenizations. Let ℐ∩\mathcal{I}_{\cap} denote this overlap set. For each position ℓ\ell, we compute co-occurrence weights between new tokens aa and old tokens bb:

(4) Wℓ(a,b)=∑i∈ℐ∩𝕀[zi,ℓnew=a]⋅𝕀[zi,ℓold=b].W_{\ell}(a,b)\;=\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\cap}}\mathbb{I}\!\left[z^{\text{new}}_{i,\ell}=a\right]\cdot\mathbb{I}\!\left[z^{\text{old}}_{i,\ell}=b\right].

We then solve a bipartite matching problem between active new and old tokens at position ℓ\ell (i.e., SID tokens observed in items from ℐ∩\mathcal{I}_{\cap}), where larger values of Wℓ​(a,b)W_{\ell}(a,b) indicate more stable correspondences. Any one-to-one assignment solver can be used to obtain ϕℓ\phi_{\ell}. In this work, we consider both a lightweight Greedy procedure and the Hungarian algorithm as possible options, with the choice of solver examined in Section 4. After matching, some new tokens may remain unmapped due to limited overlap or sparse usage. We complete ϕℓ\phi_{\ell} for all tokens used by the new assignment 𝐳new\mathbf{z}^{\text{new}} by pairing remaining new tokens with remaining (unassigned) old tokens in 𝒱ℓ\mathcal{V}_{\ell}. Finally, we rewrite all new SID sequences using Eq. (3), obtaining updated SIDs 𝐳~\tilde{\mathbf{z}} that can be directly consumed by the existing retriever checkpoint for warm-start finetuning, without retraining from scratch.

An overview of the overall alignment & finetune pipeline is shown in Figure 1.

4. Experiments

In this section, we conduct a systematic evaluation to answer the following research questions:

  • •

    RQ1: Does alignment enable warm-start finetuning after refreshing interaction-informed SIDs under temporal drift?

  • •

    RQ2: Over successive refresh-and-finetune steps, does performance remain stable or accumulate degradation?

  • •

    RQ3: What is the quality–compute trade-off of each policy, in terms of training compute (FLOPs) and alignment overhead?

4.1. Experiment Setup

4.1.1. Datasets.

We evaluate SIDs alignment policies on three public user–item benchmarks spanning e-commerce and streaming. We use Amazon Beauty (He and McAuley, 2016) as a standard e-commerce dataset in sequential recommendation. We further evaluate on VK-LSVD (Poslavsky et al., 2026), a short-video streaming benchmark. To cover a different streaming domain, we include a music streaming dataset Yambda (Ploshkin et al., 2025).

Following common practice, we apply 5-core filtering to all datasets. Table 1 reports resulting statistics.

4.1.2. Baselines.

We compare two SID paradigms: TIGER-style with content-only tokenization and LETTER-style with interaction-informed tokenization. To ensure a controlled comparison, all methods share the same generative retriever architecture and differ only in SID assignment. Both variants rely on the same RQ-VAE quantizer algorithm. Different from the original LETTER work, our implementation uses purely collaborative representations based on SASRec embeddings. We adopt a decoder-only retriever for both paradigms, rather than the encoder–decoder architecture used in the original TIGER. We make this choice deliberately to leverage autoregressive training, which reduces training FLOPs per epoch.

For each SID paradigm, we first train a Base model on an earlier time window with a fixed SID vocabulary. This checkpoint is used for all warm-started adaptations. We then compare three SID update policies: keeping stale SIDs (FT-old), rebuilding SIDs from fresh logs (FT-new), and our checkpoint-compatible alignment update (FT-ours). We also report Full, which rebuilds SIDs and trains the retriever from scratch, serving as a compute-intensive reference.

4.1.3. Evaluation protocol.

We evaluate candidate generation using Recall@K and nDCG@K metrics. Since retrieval stage is mainly responsible for providing a sufficiently large candidate pool for a downstream ranker stage, we prioritize high-recall cutoffs and report K∈{10,100,500}K\in\{10,100,500\} (capped at 500 for computational efficiency). Recall@500 serves as the main metric.

To avoid temporal leakage from leave-one-out evaluation (Ji et al., 2023; Meng et al., 2020; Gusak et al., 2025), we follow a strict chronological setup: we sort interactions by timestamp and split them into 10 contiguous blocks with an equal number of interactions. We train a Base model on blocks 1–8 and use block 9 for model selection (early stopping / epoch budget). Using selected epoch budget, we train the Full baseline on blocks 1–9 from scratch. All FT-* policies are warm-started from the Base checkpoint and use a fixed finetuning budget selected independently via a pilot update (train on blocks 1–7, finetune on block 8, select on block 9) and kept fixed across policies and datasets for a fair quality–compute comparison. This configuration intentionally targets short-horizon drift, mirroring typical industrial pipelines where finetuning is triggered frequently and the temporal gap between successive updates is relatively small.

Evaluation is performed on block 10 as a future-item-prediction task. For each user, we construct the inference context using only the recent interaction history available before block 10, i.e., the last NN interactions observed in blocks 1–9. The model then retrieves a top-KK candidate set, and items interacted with by the user during block 10 are treated as positive targets. This protocol is intended to approximate the deployment setting of industrial retrieval systems (offline scenario), where retriever operates only on historical user behavior available at inference time, while future interactions are naturally unobserved. At the same time, since evaluation is carried out on a chronologically held-out future block, it provides a measure of temporal generalization: the model must transfer from past interaction patterns to long-term user behavior under distribution shift. For a controlled comparison, we restrict histories and evaluation targets to items that are represented in the old SID vocabulary, ensuring all policies are evaluated on the same item subset (including FT-old, which cannot represent newly-created items without old SIDs). This is a conservative choice: allowing additional items introduced only in the refreshed tokenization could further improve absolute quality. We also experimented with relaxing this constraint and found that relative method performance and ranking remained consistent, suggesting that the observed patterns are not an artifact of SID vocabulary restrictions.

4.1.4. Implementation Details.

We construct SIDs using an RQ-VAE quantizer over item embeddings. For VK-LSVD and Yambda, content embeddings are provided with the datasets. For Amazon Beauty, we generate item embeddings using the same encoder and preprocessing pipeline as in (Wang et al., 2024a). For interaction-informed tokenization, we similarly follow (Wang et al., 2024a) and use trained SASRec collaborative item embeddings. TIGER and LETTER tokenization are implemented in a unified codebase, ensuring consistent retriever and quantizer architectures across variants. The baselines thus reflect key modeling choices of the original systems while abstracting away system-specific engineering.

For a generative retriever architecture we use a decoder-only Transformer with embedding dimension 128, 4 layers, 6 attention heads, feed-forward dimension 1024, ReLU activation, and dropout 0.1. For SID construction, we use an RQ-VAE tokenizer with 4 codebooks of size 512, yielding SID length 4. Both the tokenizer and the downstream retriever are trained with AdamW with learning rate 10−410^{-4} and batch size 256.

Unless stated otherwise, these hyperparameters are shared across datasets. The main dataset-specific choices are the input sequence length and the dimensionality of the item representations used for tokenization. We set the maximum input length to 20 for Amazon Beauty and to 100 for Yambda/VK-LSVD, reflecting the longer interaction histories in the streaming datasets. The RQ-VAE input dimensionality is matched to the dimensionality of the corresponding item embeddings for each dataset. Inference uses constrained beam search restricted to valid existing SIDs with beam width 500. We do not filter out previously interacted items from the model output, as such filtering is typically applied after the retrieval stage in production. For adaptation, we warm-start from the previous checkpoint, keep the learning rate fixed, and reinitialize the optimizer. We report mean metrics over 10 seeds. Significance is assessed on Recall@500 via a paired two-sided Wilcoxon test (p<0.05p<0.05). Additional reproducibility details are provided in the code implementation.33 3 Code: https://github.com/iskbaga/semantic-id-alignment

4.2. Overall Performance (RQ1)

Table 2 compares content-only and interaction-informed SIDs under rolling-origin evaluation (i.e., TIGER-style vs. LETTER-style tokenization). Base models are trained on blocks 1–8. Warm-start policies (FT-*) finetune the Base checkpoint on block 9 and differ only in how SIDs are handled during this update (old/new/ours). Full is an expensive reference that rebuilds SIDs and trains the retriever from scratch on blocks 1–9. All methods follow the same retriever architecture and training recipe. For FT-ours, we also ablate the alignment solver, using either Greedy matching or the Hungarian algorithm.

  • •

    Interaction-informed SIDs help. LETTER variants generally outperform TIGER across datasets, showing the benefit of injecting collaborative structure into SIDs.

  • •

    Alignment makes SID refresh consistently beneficial under warm-start. Without alignment, rebuilding SIDs (FT-new) is not reliably better than keeping stale SIDs (FT-old). For instance, Recall@500 decreases on Beauty (0.1573 vs. 0.1645) and Yambda (0.1100 vs. 0.1116). This suggests that an unaligned refresh can hinder warm-start adaptation: token reassignment changes the decoding space, so the model must re-learn the mapping during finetuning and may underperform the stale-SID setting. In contrast, FT-ours consistently improves high-cutoff retrieval over FT-old on all datasets, e.g., Recall@500 is 0.1756 vs. 0.1645 (Beauty), 0.1174 vs. 0.1116 (Yambda), and 0.4098 vs. 0.3512 (VK-LSVD).

  • •

    FT-ours can be competitive with full retraining. At high cutoffs, FT-ours matches or exceeds Full, (Recall@500: 0.4098 vs. 0.3910 on VK-LSVD), while Full remains best on Beauty, suggesting that the optimal refresh strategy may depend on the drift dynamics of the domain.

  • •

    Greedy vs. Hungarian. Hungarian is generally stronger (best on Beauty and Yambda), but greedy wins on VK-LSVD, making it a reasonable low-cost alternative. We assume Greedy approaches or even exceeds Hungarian as number of new block interactions increases.

4.3. Temporal Adaptation (RQ2)

In this section, we study whether SID adaptation is not only effective but also sustainable under repeated updates. Beyond one-step finetuning (RQ1), we run multi-step continual adaptation on the VK-LSVD short-video streaming benchmark.

We initialize at t=5t{=}5 by constructing LETTER-style SIDs and training on blocks 1–5. For t∈{6,7,8}t\in\{6,7,8\}, we adapt on block tt and evaluate on block t+1t{+}1.

Full constructs SIDs and trains from scratch on blocks 1–tt. FT-old finetunes on block tt with SIDs fixed from blocks 1–5. FT-new also finetunes on each new block tt but does construct fresh SIDs including this new block. FT-ours constructs SIDs at each step, iteratively aligns them to the previous token space, and finetunes on block tt. In this experiment, we use Greedy alignment.

Figure 2 illustrates the Recall@500 results across adaptation steps. FT-old suffers a steep performance decline with successive updates. Simply rebuilding the vocabulary at each step (FT-new) mitigates this degradation: by the final update it achieves substantially higher recall than FT-old. FT-ours not only consistently outperforms FT-old at every step, but also maintains a high recall level on par with Full. These results support our claim that a checkpoint-compatible SID refresh via alignment enables robust continual adaptation under temporal drift, without the need for full retraining.

4.4. Quality–Compute Trade-off (RQ3)

Beyond retrieval quality, adaptation policies differ substantially in compute cost under repeated updates. We therefore report a quality–compute trade-off on VK-LSVD using test Recall@500 and training compute in FLOPs, estimated with torch.profiler.

We report two measures: (i) Δ\DeltaTFLOPs, the additional compute to adapt from the Base checkpoint, and (ii) Total TFLOPs, the cumulative compute for a update scenario (for Full, this includes obtaining Base plus retraining from scratch on blocks 1–9). For methods that rebuild SIDs (FT-new, FT-ours, Full), FLOPs include retraining the tokenizer (quantizer) in addition to retriever training. Alignment is performed on CPU. Its overhead is analyzed below.

Let VV be the codebook size, LL the SID length, and MM the number of observed co-occurrence pairs per position (M<V2M<V^{2}). Greedy alignment sorts pairs in O⁡(M​log⁡M)O(M\log M), while Hungarian runs in O⁡(V3)O(V^{3}) per position, O⁡(L​V3)O(LV^{3}) overall. In practice, codebooks are small (V=512V=512, L=4L=4), so both are lightweight relative to GPU retriever training.

As shown in Table 3, warm-start adaptation is far cheaper than full retraining: FT-old and FT-new/FT-ours require only 2.8–3.0k TFLOPs, yielding 8.97×\times and 8.41×\times lower compute than Full, respectively. On VK-LSVD, rebuilding SIDs without alignment already improves Recall@500 over stale SIDs (FT-new: 0.3951 vs. FT-old: 0.3512) for a small extra cost (+188 TFLOPs). Finally, alignment improves the quality–compute frontier: FT-ours matches FT-new in training compute but achieves higher Recall@500 (0.4098 vs. 0.3951), while preserving compatibility with the previous SID vocabulary.

As shown in Table 3, the dominant source of computational savings is warm-start finetuning rather than the alignment step itself. In particular, FT-new and FT-ours incur nearly identical training FLOPs, because both require rebuilding SIDs and subsequently finetuning the retriever from the previous checkpoint. The benefit of alignment is instead in improving checkpoint compatibility after SID refresh: it reduces the semantic drift between consecutive SID vocabularies and helps the model adapt to refreshed tokenization while better preserving previously learned structure. As a result, FT-ours achieves higher Recall@500 than FT-new at essentially the same compute cost, thus improving the quality–compute trade-off. We therefore view alignment not as a direct compute-saving component, but as a lightweight mechanism that makes refreshed semantics easier to exploit within a warm-start adaptation pipeline. This property may be particularly useful in setups with more frequent model updates, where controlling semantic drift across successive SID refreshes could make repeated finetuning more stable and potentially reduce the optimization effort required after each update.

5. Conclusion

In this work we propose a lightweight SID alignment method to address identifier staleness in generative retrieval under temporal drift. By preserving token-space compatibility, our approach enables efficient warm-start finetuning on fresh interaction logs. Across three benchmarks, it reduces training compute by 8–9 times while improving high-cutoff recall. Future work includes an exploration of dynamic vocabulary expansion.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
